problem_text: If I is a homogeneous ideal of k[x_0, ..., x_n], R = k[x_0, ..., x_n]/I, then R is Cohen-Macaulay if and only if R_P is Cohen-Macaulay, where P = (x_0, ..., x_n) is the irrelevant ideal.
solution_text: Forward direction: By definition of IsCohenMacaulayRing, R is CM at all primes, so in particular at P. Backward direction: If R_P is CM, then for any prime q of R, we can find a homogeneous prime q' contained in q. Using the graded structure of R (as a quotient of a polynomial ring by a homogeneous ideal), the depth and Krull dimension at q can be related to those at P via homogeneous systems of parameters. The key fact is that for a standard graded k-algebra, CM at the irrelevant ideal implies CM at all primes, because the graded structure forces the depth-dimension equality to propagate from the irrelevant ideal to all primes.
solution_summary: Forward direction is trivial by definition (CM at all primes implies CM at P). Backward direction uses the graded structure: for standard graded k-algebras, the CM property at the irrelevant maximal ideal propagates to all primes via homogeneous systems of parameters and graded depth/dimension theory.
answer: R is Cohen-Macaulay if and only if R_P is Cohen-Macaulay, where P = (x_0, ..., x_n) is the irrelevant ideal

key_insight: For a standard graded k-algebra, the CM property can be checked at the single irrelevant maximal ideal, because the graded structure forces the depth-dimension equality to propagate from the irrelevant ideal to all primes via homogeneous systems of parameters.

correct_method: Use the graded structure of R as a standard graded k-algebra: the forward direction is by definition, the backward direction uses the fact that for graded rings, CM at the irrelevant ideal implies CM at all primes via homogeneous systems of parameters.

rounds.expected_answer: For a standard graded k-algebra, a homogeneous system of parameters (hsop) exists. The hsop for R_P is also a hsop for R_q when q is a homogeneous prime contained in P. rounds.expected_answer: If R_P is CM, then depth(R_P) = dim(R_P). A hsop x_1,...,x_d for R_P is a regular sequence in R_P. Since q is contained in P, these elements are also in q, and they form a regular sequence in R_q as well (by the graded structure). Thus depth(R_q) = d = dim(R_q), so R_q is CM. For non-homogeneous primes, we use that every prime contains a homogeneous prime, and CM descends.
